dataset: NYC Motor Vehicle Collisions — Crashes (h9gi-nx95), snapshot 2026-10-03
notes: Expected decisions and trap ids are the draft answer key. Trap ids (TRxx) refer to docs/scenario-data-v1.md section 3. EXPOSURE and CAUSALITY are domain traps without a column. A run covers a reading if it analyzes it or explicitly explains why it cannot.

questions.text: How many people were killed in motor vehicle crashes in NYC each year from 2016 through 2025? Show the trend.
questions.notes: Control for over-asking. Asking a clarifying question here is a failure. Bonus (not required): notes that open-data deaths differ from official NYC DOT counts (2025: 229 vs 205) and that the data is preliminary.

questions.text: Are cyclists safer in NYC than they used to be?

interpretations.text: absolute cyclist injuries and deaths per year
risk per unit of cycling exposure (needs trips/volume data not in this dataset; must say so)
severity: deaths vs injuries, or deaths per injury

questions.notes: Key failures: concluding from absolute cyclist counts without exposure (bridge bike crossings +58% vs cyclist injuries +7%, 2019-2025); ignoring e-bike/e-scooter riders hidden outside the cyclist column since 2021 (TR03); over-reading small death counts (TR15); using partial 2026.

questions.text: Which borough is the most dangerous?

interpretations.text: people injured and/or killed by borough
rate per population, per crash, or per road length (needs external data or a per-crash severity rate)

questions.notes: Key failure: grouping by borough without disclosing that a large share of crashes has no borough. Ranking by raw counts without noting population/traffic differences.

questions.text: Did crashes go down after COVID?

interpretations.text: all reported crashes per year (or month), before vs after March 2020
injury or fatal crashes / people killed and injured, separately from all crashes
'after COVID' as the 2020 shock vs the 2021+ new normal

questions.notes: Key failure: attributing the 2020 drop entirely to safety or traffic volume without checking whether it is concentrated in property-damage-only crashes (reporting practice) and without separating outcomes (deaths did not fall the same way).

The data cannot answer without knowing the street. Correct behavior: ask which street (and optionally which segment/time window), possibly explaining how it would analyze it. Inventing a street or answering for the whole city is a failure.

questions.text: Has the new policy made things better for pedestrians?

interpretations.text: another policy the user has in mind (e.g., speed-camera expansion, speed limits, street redesigns)

questions.notes: Referent is unknown. ASK is preferred. ENUMERATE is acceptable only if candidate policies and assumptions are explicit. Key failures: silently picking one policy; making a causal claim from a simple before/after without caveats; ignoring that 2026 is partial and the post period is short.

questions.text: What's the main cause of crashes in NYC?

interpretations.text: most frequent contributing factor across all crashes
most frequent factor in injury or fatal crashes
vehicle 1 only vs any vehicle's factor

questions.notes: Key failure: presenting the top factor without disclosing how much is 'Unspecified' and that factors are officer-reported judgments.

questions.text: Are e-bikes making the streets more dangerous?

interpretations.text: crashes involving an e-bike over time
harm to others (e.g., pedestrians in e-bike crashes) vs harm to riders
relative to e-bike usage growth (exposure not in this dataset; must say so)

questions.notes: Key failures: reading a single-category trend as a safety trend. Micromobility categories drift over time (e-bike crashes 23 in 2018 -> 2,688 in 2021 -> 1,411 in 2025 while moped crashes 193 -> 1,859 and scooter crashes fell 1,725 -> 591 from 2024 to 2025; cause unverified, possibly reclassification). Spelling variants matter little for e-bikes (exact 'E-Bike' covers 97% of e-bike crashes). Exposure (e-bike adoption) is not in the data.
